This routine is for people who wish to improve their size, strength, and general health without doing barbell training. Both styles of training have their advantages and disadvantages, and anyone with strong opinions on which one is better in all situations is either trying to sell you something, or they've joined a cult.The advantages of calisthenics training are, among other things- better core activation, wider variety of exercises, less stress placed on joints, faster development of tendon strength in relation to muscle strength, safety, and convenience The main disadvantages are: progression is considerably more complicated, relying on multiple factors other than the amount of weight used. The lower body is substantially harder to target, progress isn't as smooth, and it's harder to calculate 1-rep max, and hypertrophy is considerably easier. I'll assume you have no access to barbells, and include a section on creating a hybrid routine later.

If you have no experience with strength training, or are highly out of shape, I strongly suggest beginning with a calisthenic routine. The reasons for this include safety, availability, and start-up cost. Learning how to use muscles effectively is a big reason why I'm including isometric training. Most untrained athletes have trouble maintaining full-body tension under a load, or they might not fully engage muscle groups necessary for moving heavy weights. If you're overweight, losing weight is almost entirely dependent on diet, and no exercise routine will make being fat look good. If you're underweight, you will want to eat more, and stay in the hypertrophy spectrum. For beginners, I suggest full body workouts 3x a week. When you're comfortable in your training, you may add another light day for isometrics, skills, and training lagging muscle groups. I suggest staying around the 3-5 repetition range for maximum strength, 5-8 repetitions for hypertrophy, and 8-12 repetitions for hypertrophy and for when you're having trouble progressing to the next exercise. For most goals, you should shoot for a 2-1-2 tempo (2 seconds up, 1 second pause, 2 seconds down) for dynamic movements. Slower tempos rely less on momentum, and therefore involve the most strength. The exact timing doesn't matter, doing movements faster, slower, or with a longer pause is fine.. Breathing can be done any way you like, but I would suggest exhaling for increased carryover to weight training and for improved power generation in later progressions.

Skill work, set aside 5-10 minutes daily for handstand training. Handstands are useful for calisthenic training, because familiarity with the handstand increases the balance and proprioception required for more advanced movements. This doesn't need a lot of structure, but crow stands, practicing either freestanding handstands, and simply getting used to the feeling of being upside down for ~5-10 minutes will help. This can either be before the warm-up, or entirely separate from the routine.

Progression, unlike with beginner's weight training routines, calisthenics training involves manipulating multiple variables, since external loading isn't the primary source of difficulty. These include using stricter form (doing keeping your torso perfectly vertical on squats) speed (moving more slowly) increasing the number of repetitions, pausing during the rep, or holding isometric contractions in other parts of the body. You'll need to keep your entire body tense for more advanced exercises, like the one arm-push-up, so you'd might as well start practicing that.

Warm up-this is easy. Do whatever light cardio you prefer-shadowbox, skip rope, do an Irish jig, whatever- for a couple of minutes. Then do a few repetitions of the easier progressions on your routine. Don't wear yourself out. Ramping up-This frequently gets confused with the warm-up, but it's a separate concept. Pre-contracting muscles before tougher exercises will aid in performance. So while doing sets across (i.e. doing the same exercise for every work set)for example, you might do 1 set of girly push-ups, 1 set of regular push-ups, and then three work sets of diamond push-ups.

Skill Work 5-10 Minutes Handstand practice. Get used to kicking up, being upside down, bailing out, practice holding crow stands, whatever. Just fuck around with it. That's the best way to learn virtually anything.

Isometrics are the exception to the "Time under Tension" school of strength training. They do not result in any noticeable hypertrophy gains, they do however have a substantial benefit when training neuromuscular efficiency, and can be used to pre-exhaust muscles for further hypertrophy work. They are best used for training core strength, where they are superior to barbell exercises. No amount of weight training will prepare you for a back lever or a planche. The high level of muscle contraction in isometrics allows for them to build impressive *absolute strength*, within a narrow range of motion. There's a lot more to isometric training than one might ever suspect, so we'll hold off on the isometric training until the next section.

And finally, we have the strength work. Take a moment to familiarize yourself with the Prilepin's chart below, which is effectively the basis of all modern strength training:

1 RM/ %RPE |Repetitions |Reps per Workout |Effect | --- |--- |--- |--- | 95 |1-3 |7(4-10) |Max Strength | 85-95 |3-6 |10(6-14) |Strength | 75-85 |6-10|15(10-20) |Hypertrophy/Endurance | 65-75 |10-20 |18(12-24) |Plyometric Strength, Endurance, Hypertrophy | 1 RM means 1 rep max under standard training conditions, %RPE is rating of perceived exertion, since finding a bodyweight exercise you can do for just one rep is kind of silly we'll be relying on RPE to justify the set and rep schemes. Under training conditions, the two will be roughly equivalent if you're honest with yourself. Plyometric strength, or "speed strength" or "explosive power" is simply the ability to move quickly under load. "Power" without any useful qualifiers doesn't really mean anything useful in terms of physical training. If you wish to include plyometrics in the routine, they go before isometrics. They're also not recommended for beginners, since they place a lot of stress on joints and connective tissue.

We'll be mostly trying to stay in the 5-8 rep range, between strength and hypertrophy, with the exception of certain progressions might require higher training volumes. At this point(maybe earlier, but whatever) I should mention that the chart does not distinguish between *Neuromuscular* and *Biomechanical* efficiency.

So we have the basic structure of the routine:

Skill work

Warm-up

Isometrics (Not "work" because work equals force times distance.)

Strength Work

Hypertrophy Work

The skill work, isometrics, can be done separately from the main routine, or even skipped entirely. Hypertrophy work is almost completely superfluous and honestly if your main goal is to put on mass, you should just go to a gym.

Cardio, with the exception of sprints, should not be done within an hour of doing the strength exercises.
